content.overview: Light duration, spectral distribution, fixture geometry and canopy architecture interact with crop development. Specialists should interpret these variables together while keeping photobiology claims proportional to the evidence.

vocabulary.definition: The distribution of emitted light across wavelengths.
A developmental response influenced by the duration and timing of light and dark periods.
The spatial arrangement of leaves, stems and branches that affects interception, shading and measurement geometry.

sections.title: Duration is biologically meaningful
sections.body: Photoperiod is not only part of a DLI calculation; it can influence developmental signaling. Facility schedules therefore should not be changed solely to chase a photon total.

sections.title: Spectrum and intensity are different dimensions
sections.body: A spectral description does not replace PPFD measurement, and a PPFD value does not describe spectral composition. Record which question the measurement is answering.

sections.title: Canopy architecture changes interception
sections.body: Training, plant spacing and developmental stage affect shading and distribution. Repeated mapping should use a defined crop plane and note major architecture changes.

workedExamples: Two fixtures can produce similar PPFD at one point but differ in spectrum and distribution; those systems should not be considered equivalent from one measurement alone.
commonMistakes: Treating one spectrum as universally optimal.
Using DLI to ignore photoperiod biology.
Comparing maps after major canopy changes without recording the change.
content.practicalApplication: Review a mock change in photoperiod, fixture spectrum and canopy height and identify which measurements are needed before attributing a crop response to one variable.
content.summary: Advanced lighting interpretation separates intensity, duration, spectrum and canopy geometry while considering how they interact.
